305K The night of January 27 exposed a troubling reality inside Maharaja Tej Singh District Hospital in Mainpuri, Uttar Pradesh - one of the district’s primary government healthcare facilities. Amid rainfall in the region, the hospital reportedly suffered a sudden power outage. What followed raised serious questions about preparedness. Emergency services were forced to continue treatment in near darkness after backup systems, including inverter support and a generator, allegedly failed to function on time. ⚡🏥 Visuals that later surfaced showed doctors and medical staff treating patients using mobile phone torchlights. In the emergency ward, phone beams became the only source of light as injured patients waited for care. For families standing nearby, the scene was unsettling - a government hospital struggling with the most basic requirement: electricity. 📱🩺 Patients and attendants reportedly expressed fear and anger, questioning how a district hospital could be left without reliable backup power during emergencies. Many pointed out that electricity is not an added facility but a critical necessity for safe medical treatment. Hospital authorities were informed, and power supply was eventually restored after the generator was started. Senior officials said the incident was being reviewed and that responsibility would be fixed for the lapse. An internal inquiry has been mentioned to assess why emergency power systems failed when they were needed most. The incident has once again highlighted gaps in public health infrastructure, especially in district-level hospitals meant to serve large populations. Beyond viral visuals and public outrage, it raises a deeper concern - when systems fail, doctors improvise, but patients pay the price. For many, the blackout was not just a technical failure. It was a reminder that healthcare infrastructure, not paperwork, saves lives. #gajabkiduniyaa #Mainpuri #DistrictHospital #PowerFailure #HealthcareCrisis #EmergencyCare #UPNews #PatientSafety #HealthInfrastructure #GovtHospital #IndiaNews #Accountability #GroundReality

33.9K Darkness in the 'World's Fourth-Largest Economy': Mainpuri Hospital Incident Exposes UP's Healthcare Crisis On January 27, 2026, a viral video from Maharaja Tej Singh District Hospital in Mainpuri, Uttar Pradesh, shocked the nation. Amid heavy rainfall causing a power outage, doctors and staff treated patients—including emergency cases—using only mobile phone flashlights. Backup systems like inverters and generators reportedly failed, leaving the facility in near darkness for nearly two hours. Staff improvised with phone lights to perform examinations and procedures, highlighting a desperate reliance on personal devices in a government hospital. This incident is not isolated but symptomatic of systemic failures under the Uttar Pradesh BJP government. Despite claims of massive investments in health schemes like Ayushman Bharat and boasts of economic progress, public hospitals continue to suffer from inadequate infrastructure, non-functional backup power, poor maintenance, and shortages of essential facilities. Recurring issues—power cuts, unhygienic conditions, and equipment breakdowns—reveal neglect in emergency preparedness and basic governance. Critics argue that while funds are allocated, ground-level execution falters, eroding public trust and endangering lives. Such events underscore the irony: a state projecting digital and economic advancement fails to ensure reliable electricity and healthcare in its own facilities. The Mainpuri episode demands accountability and urgent reforms. #MainpuriHospital #UPHealthcare #BJPFailures #PowerOutage #SystemicNeglect UttarPradesh PublicHealthCrisis YogiAdityanath

5,271 A tragic incident in Chhatarpur district of Madhya Pradesh has once again raised serious questions about emergency healthcare in India. A 65-year-old man, Jagdish Vishwakarma, suffered severe chest pain suspected to be a heart attack. With no ambulance available, his family rushed him to the district hospital in a loader vehicle while his son kept giving CPR on the way. Traffic delays slowed them down further. By the time they reached the hospital, doctors declared him brought dead. The incident shows how delays in emergency response can cost lives. India’s healthcare system continues to face serious challenges. The country has only about 1–1.3 hospital beds per 1,000 people, which is below global standards. There is an estimated shortage of nearly 20 lakh hospital beds, especially in rural areas where around 65% of the population lives. India also has roughly 20 health workers per 10,000 people, far below international recommendations. In emergency care, the country operates around 17,000–20,000 ambulances, but only about 3,000–3,400 are Advanced Life Support (ALS) units equipped for critical cases. Public health spending remains around 1.5–2% of GDP, and more than 50% of healthcare expenses are paid directly by families, putting heavy financial pressure on households. These gaps in infrastructure, staffing, and emergency services make timely treatment difficult, especially in life-threatening situations like heart attacks. #madhyapradeshnews #madhyapradeshnewslive #indiahealthcare #healthcarecrisis #poverty #povertyinindia #vishwaguru

Source: https://www.newindianexpress.com/states/tamil-nadu/2019/May/08/three-madurai-state-hospital-patients-on-life-support-die-within-10-minutes-during-power-outage-1974272.html
Title: Three Madurai hospital patients on life support die during power outage
Chunks: 0,1
MADURAI: Three patients who were admitted to the Neuro Intensive Care Unit (ward number 101) at the Government Rajaji Hospital died on Tuesday night, allegedly due to lack of oxygen supply when the hospital faced power outage due to rain in the city. The relatives alleged that the ventilators stopped working while the hospital management claimed that the ventilators continued to function on battery back-up. The deceased have been identified as G Ravindran, M Malliga and P Palaniammal.
According to hospital sources, G Ravindran (52) of Srivilliputhur was admitted at the GRH on May 3 after he suffered head injuries due to an accidental fall. He was recuperating from surgery which was performed on him on Monday.
Another patient, M Malliga (58) of Melur was admitted on Monday, after being referred from Velammal Hospital. She had undergone surgery for an aneurysm at the private hospital on April 18 and was on life support since admission at GRH.
A resident of Ottanchathiram, P Palaniammal (60) who suffered a skull bone fracture in a road traffic accident on May 3 was admitted at the GRH on May 5.
According to the relatives of the deceased patients, the annexe block of GRH near Anna Bus Stand (Trauma Care Centre) had a power outage from 5.30 pm till 7.15 pm. They stated that the hospital's power generator failed, which the hospital Dean Dr K Vanitha admitted.
During the outage, the ventilators stopped working leading to lack of oxygen supply. The patients suffered from breathlessness and died within minutes while the power was still out, alleged the relatives of the deceased.
Refuting the allegations, Dr Vanitha said that the generator tripped mid-way and stopped functioning. "But, the ventilators are equipped to function to a maximum of two hours using battery back-up, in the absence of power supply," she pointed. According to the hospital, Malliga passed away at 6.55 pm, Ravindran died at 7 pm and Palaniammal at 7.05 pm.
Stating the cause of death, she said that all the three patients died after developing cardio-pulmonary arrest which she said is a common complication in case of patients with head injuries.

Following the incident, an autopsy is to be performed on the bodies of the three patients and a detailed report about the incident is to be submitted to the Health Secretary Beela Rajesh.

MADURAI: Three patients who were admitted to the Neuro Intensive Care Unit (ward number 101) at the Government Rajaji Hospital died on Tuesday night, allegedly due to lack of oxygen supply when the hospital faced power outage due to rain in the city. The relatives alleged that the ventilators stopped working while the hospital management claimed that the ventilators continued to function on battery back-up. The deceased have been identified as G Ravindran, M Malliga and P Palaniammal.
According to hospital sources, G Ravindran (52) of Srivilliputhur was admitted at the GRH on May 3 after he suffered head injuries due to an accidental fall. He was recuperating from surgery which was performed on him on Monday.
Another patient, M Malliga (58) of Melur was admitted on Monday, after being referred from Velammal Hospital. She had undergone surgery for an aneurysm at the private hospital on April 18 and was on life support since admission at GRH.
A resident of Ottanchathiram, P Palaniammal (60) who suffered a skull bone fracture in a road traffic accident on May 3 was admitted at the GRH on May 5.
According to the relatives of the deceased patients, the annexe block of GRH near Anna Bus Stand (Trauma Care Centre) had a power outage from 5.30 pm till 7.15 pm. They stated that the hospital's power generator failed, which the hospital Dean Dr K Vanitha admitted.
During the outage, the ventilators stopped working leading to lack of oxygen supply. The patients suffered from breathlessness and died within minutes while the power was still out, alleged the relatives of the deceased.
Refuting the allegations, Dr Vanitha said that the generator tripped mid-way and stopped functioning. "But, the ventilators are equipped to function to a maximum of two hours using battery back-up, in the absence of power supply," she pointed. According to the hospital, Malliga passed away at 6.55 pm, Ravindran died at 7 pm and Palaniammal at 7.05 pm.
Stating the cause of death, she said that all the three patients died after developing cardio-pulmonary arrest which she said is a common complication in case of patients with head injuries.
texts.1: Following the incident, an autopsy is to be performed on the bodies of the three patients and a detailed report about the incident is to be submitted to the Health Secretary Beela Rajesh.

# Insights from Uganda's ESOs
## Uploaded by
“The whole is greater than the sum of its parts” is a phrase associated with the principles behi nd entrepreneurship ecosystem development. When ecosystem actors collaborate, the value they create by working together is larger than if they work independently. This certainly rings true with what we’ve experienced working with more than 170 fellow Entrepreneur Support Organisations (ESOs) from 40 countries since 2015. Village Capital’s mission is to unlock capital for early-stage entrepreneurs building emergent solutions for global social, economic, and environmental challenges. We have a 12-year track record and have supported more seed-stage, i mpact-driven entrepreneurs than any other incubator or accelerator in the world. Our work with other ESOs reﬂects our commitment to being part of a community that works together to create more value for entrepreneurs. Sub-Saharan Africa is a hub for innovation. The continent has the highest rate of entrepreneurshipglobally, partly because of its young and digitally literate population. The support provided by tech hubs, incubators, and accelerators is invaluable. Depending on which resources you reference, Afric a has somewhere between 600 to 1300 of these organisations across the continent and they provide the contextualised support that African entrepreneurs need to grow and scale.These organisations – and the people who run them – are often under-resourced. As a result, many are short-staﬀed and overwhelmed, making it harder to run eﬀective programs or keep their doors open.

# Insights from Uganda's ESOs
## Uploaded by
“The whole is greater than the sum of its parts” is a phrase associated with the principles behi nd entrepreneurship ecosystem development. When ecosystem actors collaborate, the value they create by working together is larger than if they work independently. This certainly rings true with what we’ve experienced working with more than 170 fellow Entrepreneur Support Organisations (ESOs) from 40 countries since 2015. Village Capital’s mission is to unlock capital for early-stage entrepreneurs building emergent solutions for global social, economic, and environmental challenges. We have a 12-year track record and have supported more seed-stage, i mpact-driven entrepreneurs than any other incubator or accelerator in the world. Our work with other ESOs reﬂects our commitment to being part of a community that works together to create more value for entrepreneurs. Sub-Saharan Africa is a hub for innovation. The continent has the highest rate of entrepreneurshipglobally, partly because of its young and digitally literate population. The support provided by tech hubs, incubators, and accelerators is invaluable. Depending on which resources you reference, Afric a has somewhere between 600 to 1300 of these organisations across the continent and they provide the contextualised support that African entrepreneurs need to grow and scale.These organisations – and the people who run them – are often under-resourced. As a result, many are short-staﬀed and overwhelmed, making it harder to run eﬀective programs or keep their doors open.
What’s working in entrepreneur support in Uganda?
